title: Building Reusable CLI Commands
keywords: cli tools, background jobs, and automation
learning_outcomes: Explain what building reusable cli commands contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: command organization.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: CLI scripts and background jobs need explicit inputs, predictable exit behavior, bounded resource use, observable failures, and safe retry semantics. Long-running work should not rely on a browser request staying open. In this lesson, focus on command organization; then compare it with option parsing. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use building reusable cli commands when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: CLI scripts and background jobs need explicit inputs, predictable exit behavior, bounded resource use, observable failures, and safe retry semantics. Long-running work should not rely on a browser request staying open. For building reusable cli commands, begin with command organization. Also distinguish option parsing; output formatting; configuration. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Building Reusable CLI Commands
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$required = ["DATABASE_URL", "APP_KEY"];
$provided = ["DATABASE_URL" => "configured", "APP_KEY" => "configured"];
echo count(array_intersect($required, array_keys($provided))) . " settings present" . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for building reusable cli commands from top to bottom. Start by identifying command organization, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
